info.name: Chat Stack — Timeout Scenarios (Stage)
info.description:
Drives the shortened stage-only timeout/resilience config seeded by `V168__common_modulith_stage_fast_timeouts_for_qa.sql` against `ChattingOrchestrationSecureController` (`/api/v1/secure/chatting/orchestration`).

## Setup
1. Set `base_url` to the stage modulith host (default below is the stage fallback host from `application-stage.properties`).
2. Get `access_token` + `visit_id` - two ways:
   - Automated (recommended): set `auth_email` to a real email with stage visit history, run A1 (sends an OTP to that inbox), set `otp_code` from the email, run A2 (saves `access_token`), then run A3 (resolves + saves `visit_id`). Same email-OTP flow this frontend uses. See folder A. Auth (User A).
   - Manual: if you already have a valid bearer JWT and visit UUID from another source, just set `access_token` / `visit_id` directly and skip folder A.
3. Run both requests in **0. Shared — Create Conversation + Start Orchestration** once per scenario folder — `conversationId` is not something you make up client-side (`.../orchestration/conversations/{id}/start` 404s unless that conversation already exists and is owned by your token), so **Create conversation** creates a real one first and saves it as the `conversation_id` collection variable, then **Start orchestration** correlates onto it.
4. (Optional, only needed for folder 4) Repeat step 2 for a SECOND, different email/user via folder **B. Auth (User B)** (`auth_email_2`/`otp_code_2` -> `access_token_2`/`visit_id_2`), then run **0b. Shared (User B)** — see folder 4's description for why a lone client can't cleanly trigger bulkhead exhaustion.

## Which scenarios Postman can actually drive
- **Wait-based** (idle timeout, SSE emitter timeout, replay-cache window): fully drivable — either via each folder's own pre-request `setTimeout` delay (Postman v10+ sandbox) or by running the folder in the **Collection Runner** with an inter-request **Delay** set as noted in each folder's description. For idle timeout specifically, confirmed on stage: the actual trigger point is ~19s after the session's `startedAt`, not exactly the configured `PT15S` (the timer only arms once the process reaches its wait-gateway, after the agent's first turn finishes) — folders 1 and 7 wait 30s to give a safe margin.
- **Concurrency-based** (bulkhead exhaustion, per-client rate limit, max concurrent SSE streams): drivable via a pre-request script that fires several `pm.sendRequest` calls fire-and-forget immediately before the visible request goes out. This is best-effort — exact timing isn't guaranteed over HTTP, so an occasional run may not trigger the rejection; re-run if so. For guaranteed concurrency, fire the same request N times in parallel from Newman/curl instead.
- **LLM-latency-dependent** (classifier call-timeout, classifier circuit breaker, summarizer call-timeout): NOT deterministically triggerable from Postman — these only fire when the real OpenAI call happens to exceed the shortened budget (3s / 10s). The relevant folders build the preconditions (multi-route persona input, long conversation history) and note what to grep for in logs; whether the timeout actually fires depends on live model latency.
- **Infra-dependent** (Camunda join-timeout + retry exhaustion, HTTP-connector connect/read timeout): NOT achievable from Postman at all — they require actually degrading Zeebe or the modulith pod itself. See the **9. Infra-Dependent (not Postman-drivable)** folder for what to do operationally instead.

## Status codes / log lines to watch for
- `503` body code `SERVLET_BOUND_TIMEOUT` — servlet-bound Camunda wait exceeded or bulkhead full (`ServletBoundedCamundaMessagePublisher`).
- `429` body code `PER_CLIENT_RATE_LIMIT` — per-client Camunda admission budget exhausted (`PerClientRateLimiterGuard`).
- A follow-up after idle timeout does NOT fail — confirmed on real stage: it transparently rolls over into a fresh session (`202`, no client-visible error). Confirm the rollover directly via `GET /v1/internal/chatting/conversations/{id}/sessions` (a second session row, new `processInstanceKey`) rather than the response code; `[step-svc] markSessionTerminal ... terminal=true` in the logs is the equivalent signal if you have log access instead.
- `chatting.camunda.servlet_bound_timeout`, `chatting.camunda.per_client_rate_limited`, `chatting.classifier.timeout`, `chatting.classifier.circuit_open` — Micrometer counters to check on the metrics endpoint or dashboards during a run.

request.description:
Set `auth_email` first. This is a public endpoint (`auth: noauth` overrides the collection's bearer auth, which would otherwise send a stale/empty token here). Sends the OTP email as a side effect and reports whether this email is eligible (`data.eligible`, `data.reasons`, `data.personas`) — mirrors `otpAccessTokenFlow.js#prepareOtpChallenge` from this frontend (DEV/TEST/STAGE all use this same public flow; only LOCAL has an extra provisioning call first).

After this succeeds, check the `auth_email` inbox for the OTP code, paste it into the `otp_code` collection variable, then run **A2**.

Exchanges the OTP for a real bearer token and saves it as the `access_token` collection variable (and `refresh_token`, if the response includes one) — mirrors `otpAccessTokenFlow.js#exchangeOtpForToken`. The code is short-lived and single-use; if this fails, re-run **A1** for a fresh one.

'(post-login sync can lag), or manually set `visit_id` to a known visit UUID for this user.');

request.description:
Run **A2** first. Uses the collection's bearer auth (`{{access_token}}`, now populated by A2) to list this user's visits and saves the first `visitId` found as the `visit_id` collection variable — mirrors `visitResolution.js#fetchVisitIdFromMyVisitsLists` (this frontend also falls back to `/my-visits/upcoming` and `/my-visits/past` if `/my-visits` alone comes back empty; re-run this request a couple of times if the first attempt is empty, since post-login visit sync can lag a few seconds).

Once this succeeds, `access_token` and `visit_id` are both set and you can proceed to **0. Shared** below.

exec: console.warn('No visits found for User B yet — re-run in a few seconds, or set `visit_id_2` manually.');

request.description:
Run **B2** first. Uses `access_token_2` explicitly (auth set to `noauth` + manual header, since the collection-level bearer auth defaults to `access_token`, not `_2`). Saves the first `visitId` found as `visit_id_2`.

Once this succeeds, `access_token_2` and `visit_id_2` are both set for folder 4's two-user bulkhead test.

`conversationId` is NOT something you make up client-side — `.../orchestration/conversations/{id}/start` requires a conversation row that already exists and is owned by this token (`ChattingEntityLoader#requireConversationForClientUpdate` 404s otherwise). This creates a real conversation (+ its initial session) on `ChattingSecureController` and saves the returned id as the `conversation_id` collection variable. Run this BEFORE **Start orchestration** below, and before every scenario folder that follows — none of them generate their own conversation id anymore.

Run **Create conversation** immediately before this request (same folder). Correlates the first message onto that conversation's freshly-created session, seeding `idleTimeoutDuration` etc. from `ChattingOrchestrationProperties.Process` into the Camunda process. Run both requests in this folder first, in order, before any scenario folder below.

item.name: 0b. Shared (User B) — Create Conversation + Start Orchestration (only for folder 4)

request.description: Same as **0. Shared**'s Create conversation, but for a SECOND, different user (`access_token_2`) — needed only for folder **4. Camunda Servlet-Bound Bulkhead Exhaustion**. Auth is set to `noauth` at the request level (so the collection's `{{access_token}}` bearer auth isn't also injected on top) and the `Authorization: Bearer {{access_token_2}}` header is set manually instead. Saves the result to `conversation_id_b`.

Run **Create conversation (User B)** immediately before this request. Correlates onto User B's freshly-created session, using `visit_id_2` (must be owned by `access_token_2`'s user). Only needed for folder 4.

exec: // Postman v10+ sandbox supports async pre-request scripts.
// Sleeps 30s. Confirmed on stage 2026-08-30: the timer only starts once the
// process reaches its wait-gateway, AFTER the agent's first turn finishes
// processing, so it actually fires ~19s after startedAt, not exactly PT15S.
// A 16s wait was tested and confirmed too short (session still ACTIVE, no
pm.test('session already idle-timed-out -> follow-up transparently rolls over (still accepted)', function () {

request.description:
Run both requests in **0. Shared** first (Create conversation, then Start orchestration), then run this one. Its pre-request script sleeps 30s before sending the follow-up.

If your Postman version doesn't support async pre-request scripts, delete the sleep script and instead run this 2-request sequence (Start, then this) via **Collection Runner** with the inter-request **Delay** set to 30000ms.

**Confirmed on real stage, 2026-08-30**, using the internal endpoint `GET /v1/internal/chatting/conversations/{id}/sessions` (no JWT needed — network-trust only): the old session transitions to `TIMED_OUT` ~19s after its `startedAt`, not exactly the configured `PT15S` — the timer only starts once the process reaches its wait-gateway, *after* the agent's first turn finishes processing (BeginTurn -> classify -> LLM/tool-call turn -> CompleteTurn), which adds a few seconds. A follow-up sent after that point creates a genuinely NEW session (a different `processInstanceKey`) via `SessionLifecycleService.startOrPublishAfterRollover`, while the old session stays `TIMED_OUT` untouched — confirmed directly, not inferred. Both the old and new session return the same `202` to the client either way; use the internal endpoint above to see which one actually happened, not the response code.

**Known failure mode (tested and confirmed):** waiting only 16s undershoots the real trigger point — the session is still `ACTIVE` at that point and the follow-up publishes onto it normally, no rollover. Use 30s, not 16s.

**Verify in logs (if you have access):** `[step-svc] markSessionTerminal ... terminal=true`.

Run both requests in **0. Shared** first. Postman can open this SSE stream and show events as they arrive, but grading exact close timing from a test script is unreliable — time it manually (stopwatch / Postman's response timer) or via `curl -N` for precision.

**Scenario A — emitter timeout (20s):** send a follow-up that forces multi-step tool-call latency (e.g. a catering order needing catalogue lookup + confirmation) so the turn takes >20s. The stream should close at ~20s (`sse.emitter-timeout-ms` = `spring.mvc.async.request-timeout` = 20000).

**Scenario B — replay cache (45s):** immediately after the stream above closes, re-open this same request within 45s — expect the last terminal event replayed instantly (`ResponseReplayCache`). Wait past 45s (`hardening.response-cache-expire-after-write` = PT45S) before reconnecting a second time — expect no replay, just a fresh wait.

**Verify in logs:** a timeout shows as `SSE stream failed to open` / emitter completion in `AgentChatResponseSseEmitterFactory` / `AgentResponsePushService`.

item.name: 3. Max Concurrent SSE Streams Per User (sse.max-emitters-per-user = 2)

exec: // AgentResponsePushService keeps only ONE live emitter per conversationId (a 2nd
// subscribe on the same id REPLACES the 1st instead of racing it for the per-user
// cap). So this creates+starts 2 MORE conversations for the SAME user first, then
// opens 2 fire-and-forget streams on those, leaving the visible request below to
// open the 3rd stream on the original {{conversation_id}} from folder 0.
body: { mode: 'raw', raw: JSON.stringify({ initialTitle: label, initialSummary: null }) }
chatContext: { schemaVersion: '1.0', contextType: 'VISIT', contextData: { id: visitId } },
// Fire these 2 fire-and-forget (not awaited) so they stay open concurrently with
// the visible request instead of completing before it goes out.
console.log('burst stream', i, res && res.code, err);

request.description:
Run both requests in **0. Shared** first. This request's pre-request script needs an async-capable Postman sandbox (v10+): it awaits creating+starting 2 MORE conversations for the same user, opens fire-and-forget streams on those two, then this visible request opens the 3rd stream on the original `conversation_id` — 3 different conversations, same user, exceeding `sse.max-emitters-per-user` = 2.

Using 3 different conversations (not 3 opens on one id) matters: `AgentResponsePushService` keeps only one live emitter per conversationId, so opening a 2nd stream on the SAME id would just replace the 1st (`REPLACED_PRIOR_EMITTER`) instead of racing it against the per-user cap.

Best-effort timing — over real network latency the 3 calls may not land perfectly concurrently; re-run if all 3 succeed. For a guaranteed test, log in as the same user in 3 separate browser tabs/devices and open 3 different conversations' streams instead.

**Verify in logs:** `AgentResponsePushService` logging the per-user emitter cap being hit (`REJECTED_CAP`).

item.name: 4. Camunda Servlet-Bound Bulkhead Exhaustion (pool=1, queue=2 -> max 3 in-flight)

exec: // PerClientRateLimiterGuard.acquireOrThrow(clientId) runs at the top of BOTH start()
// and sendAgentReply(), sharing ONE 2-per-5s budget PER CLIENT. A single client's
// 4-call burst would get rate-limited down to at most 2 calls before ever reaching
// the bulkhead, so this needs a SECOND, different user (access_token_2 /
// conversation_id_b, from folder 0b) so neither user's own rate limit interferes
// with a genuine 4-way race for the bulkhead's shared capacity of 3.
console.warn('access_token_2 / conversation_id_b not set — run 0b. Shared (User B) first. ' +
'Falling back to 3 extra calls from the SAME user as a degraded, best-effort test: ' +
'expect PER_CLIENT_RATE_LIMIT (429) on most of these rather than a clean bulkhead signal.');
const body = JSON.stringify({ followUpInput: 'burst message (single-user fallback)', displayText: null, clientMessageId: null });
console.log('burst follow-up (fallback)', i, res && res.code, err);
// 1 extra fire-and-forget from User A (the visible request below is A's 2nd), plus
// 2 fire-and-forget from User B -> 4 total, 2 per user, each within that user's own budget.
body: { mode: 'raw', raw: JSON.stringify({ followUpInput: 'bulkhead burst ' + r.label, displayText: null, clientMessageId: null }) }
console.log('burst follow-up', r.label, res && res.code, err);
pm.test('this call (User A, 2nd) is likely rejected as SERVLET_BOUND_TIMEOUT (503) - best effort', function () {

request.description:
Setup for this folder specifically:
1. Run both requests in **0. Shared** (User A).
2. Set `access_token_2` + `visit_id_2` to a second, different user, and run both requests in **0b. Shared (User B)**.
3. WAIT at least 6 seconds (past the 5s per-client rate-limit window) before sending this request, so both users' budgets are fully fresh for the burst.

This request's pre-request script fires 1 more call from User A + 2 calls from User B via `pm.sendRequest`, then this visible request is User A's 2nd — 4 total, 2 per user, racing the shared `camundaServletBound` bulkhead (pool=1 + queue=2 = 3 max in-flight, all operations across the whole app share this one pool regardless of which user or conversation they belong to).

Without `access_token_2`/`conversation_id_b` set, the script falls back to a single-user 3-call burst, but that's a degraded test — `PerClientRateLimiterGuard` (2 calls per 5s per client) will very likely reject 2 of those 3 with `429 PER_CLIENT_RATE_LIMIT` before they ever reach the bulkhead, so you may not see the bulkhead reject anything at all. The two-user path above is the one that actually isolates this scenario.

Best-effort timing over HTTP either way — if nothing gets rejected, re-run, or use the k6 script (`docs/k6/chat-stack-concurrency.k6.js`) for a deterministic version of this same test.

**Expect:** at least one call gets `503` body code `SERVLET_BOUND_TIMEOUT`.

**Verify in logs/metrics:** `[camunda-bounded] ... rejected — pool/queue full (pool=1, capacity=2)`; metric `chatting.camunda.servlet_bound_timeout`.

exec: const body = JSON.stringify({ followUpInput: 'rate-limit burst', displayText: null, clientMessageId: null });
// Fire 2 fire-and-forget follow-ups first; this request's own call is the 3rd within the 5s window.
console.log('rate-limit burst', i, res && res.code, err);
pm.test('3rd call within 5s is likely rate-limited (429) - best effort', function () {

request.description:
Run both requests in **0. Shared** first. This is the same authenticated user (`clientId` = JWT user id) sending a 3rd Camunda-message call inside a 5-second window — exceeding `per-client-rate-limit-per-period` = 2.

Unlike bulkhead exhaustion, this is per-user, so 3 calls from the SAME token within 5s is what matters — the burst here doesn't need to race with other users.

**Expect:** `429` body code `PER_CLIENT_RATE_LIMIT` on the call(s) beyond the 2-per-5s budget.

**Verify in logs/metrics:** `Camunda per-client rate limit exceeded`; metric `chatting.camunda.per_client_rate_limited`.

item.name: 6. Classifier LLM Timeout & Circuit Breaker (call-timeout=3s, wait-in-open=5s) — load-dependent

request.description:
NOT deterministically triggerable from Postman — the classifier only runs (and can only time out) when the persona has 2+ reachable routes (`PersonaRouteRegistry.allowedRoutes` > 1); a single-route persona short-circuits and skips the LLM call entirely. Use a persona/context known to have multiple routes for this to have any chance of firing.

Run this request repeatedly (Collection Runner, 20-30 iterations, 0 delay) to generate load — whether `classifier-llm.call-timeout` (3s) or the circuit breaker (`wait-duration-in-open-state` = 5s after `failureRateThreshold`=50% over `slidingWindowSize`=20 calls) actually trips depends on real OpenAI response latency at the time, not anything Postman controls.

**Expect on timeout:** classification silently falls back to the persona's fallback route rather than erroring the request.

**Verify in logs/metrics:** `[classifier] timed out after 3s — falling back to ...` / `chatting.classifier.timeout`; breaker trip: `[classifier] circuit breaker CLOSED -> OPEN` / `chatting.classifier.circuit_open`, then `-> HALF_OPEN` ~5s later.

item.name: Build long history, then re-start to trigger rollover

exec: // See folder 1's finding: the idle timer fires ~19s after startedAt, not
// exactly PT15S, and 16s was confirmed too short. 30s gives a safe margin.

request.description:
Procedure for this folder (uses the SAME `conversation_id` throughout — do NOT run folder 0 again in between):
1. Run both requests in **0. Shared** once (Create conversation, then Start orchestration) to seed `conversation_id`.
2. Send 10-15 follow-ups on that same conversation (reuse the folder-2 "Follow-up" request body, or run it via Collection Runner with several iterations) to build up conversation history — bigger history means a bigger summarization prompt.
3. Run THIS request last. Its pre-request script waits 30s (confirmed on stage: the idle timer actually fires ~19s after the session's `startedAt`, not exactly PT15S — 16s was tested and found too short) so the prior session is no longer ACTIVE, then calls `/start` again on the same `conversation_id` — `SessionLifecycleService.startOrPublishAfterRollover` detects the non-ACTIVE session and rolls over, which asynchronously triggers `SessionResumeSummarizer` on the closed session. To confirm the rollover actually happened rather than guessing, check `GET /v1/internal/chatting/conversations/{id}/sessions` for a second session row.

NOT deterministically triggerable — whether the summarization call actually exceeds `summarizer-llm.call-timeout` (10s, down from the default 60s) depends on real OpenAI latency for that prompt size, not anything Postman controls. A bigger history in step 2 raises the odds.

**Expect on timeout:** summary write is skipped silently (empty summary) — no user-facing error, since this runs async after commit.

**Verify in logs:** `[resume-summarizer] LLM call timed out after 10s`.

These two shortened-timeout scenarios cannot be forced from Postman alone — they require actual infrastructure slowness/unavailability, not client-side request patterns:

**Camunda join-timeout (3s) + retry exhaustion (retry-max-attempts=1):** needs Zeebe itself to be slow or briefly unreachable — e.g. restart/scale down the Zeebe broker or gateway pod in stage during a test call to `user-messages` or `start`. Expect the servlet thread to fail fast in ~3s (single attempt, no retry) with `503 SERVLET_BOUND_TIMEOUT`, instead of the old ~183s retry budget. Verify via log `Camunda correlate failed after 1 attempts` / `Camunda publish failed after 1 attempts`.

**HTTP-connector timeout (connect/read = 3s each):** bounds Camunda's HTTP-JSON connector calling back into the modulith's own internal endpoints. Trigger by making an internal tool call slow (e.g. a downstream ACL-proxy or servicerequests call under load) or by restarting the modulith pod mid-request so the connector can't connect within 3s. Check the specific BPMN service task's configured `retries`/`retryBackoff` for what happens next.

This request is just a harmless health-check placeholder so the folder isn't empty — replace/ignore it once you're driving these scenarios operationally instead of via Postman.
